title: Maggard v. State
description: Whether the filing of a referendum petition automatically suspends a legislative act (House Bill No. 1) under article III, sections 49, 52(a), or 52(b) of the Missouri Constitution, or if suspension only occurs after the petition's sufficiency is certified.
plaintiff_argument: The filing of the referendum petition on December 9, 2025, automatically suspended HB 1 under the Missouri Constitution, and statutes permitting the secretary to delay suspension until certification are unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: The filing of the referendum petition does not automatically suspend HB 1; the law remains in effect until the petition is certified as sufficient through the statutory process, which determines if it meets constitutional signature requirements.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, concluding that the December 9 referendum petition filing did not automatically suspend House Bill No. 1 under the Missouri Constitution.

title: Wise v. State; Healey v. State
description: Whether the 2025 congressional redistricting map enacted by the Missouri legislature violates article III, section 45 of the Missouri Constitution by failing to meet requirements for compactness, contiguity, and equal population.
plaintiff_argument: The 2025 Map violates article III, section 45 of the Missouri Constitution because the congressional districts are not compact, not contiguous, and not of nearly equal population, specifically citing issues with districts 4, 5, 6 and voting tabulation district KC 811.
defendant_argument: The 2025 Map complies with article III, section 45 of the Missouri Constitution, as it meets the requirements for compactness, contiguity, and equal population, and is statistically more compact than previous maps.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Missouri affirmed the circuit court's judgment, finding that the Appellants failed to prove the 2025 Map violates the Missouri Constitution's requirements for congressional redistricting.

title: Luther v. Hoskins
description: Whether House Bill 1, which repealed congressional districts adopted in 2022 and established new ones without a new census, violates article III, section 45 of the Missouri Constitution by allowing mid-decade redistricting.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that HB 1 is unconstitutional because article III, section 45 limits the General Assembly to a single congressional redistricting following census certification, implying a prohibition on mid-decade redistricting.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that HB 1 is constitutional because article III, section 45 obligates redistricting after a census but does not prohibit more frequent redistricting, as the General Assembly has plenary legislative power unless expressly restrained.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, declaring House Bill 1 valid and concluding that article III, section 45 of the Missouri Constitution does not limit the General Assembly's plenary legislative power to enact HB 1.

title: Fitz-James v. Hoskins
description: Whether House Joint Resolution 73 (HJR 73) violates the Missouri Constitution's single subject rule, and whether its proposed summary statement and fair ballot language are fair and sufficient to inform voters about its effects, including the repeal of a voter-approved reproductive freedom amendment and new restrictions on abortion and gender transition procedures.
plaintiff_argument: HJR 73 violates the single subject rule by combining disparate topics (reproductive health, gender transition, litigation rules). Additionally, its ballot language is misleading and insufficient, failing to clearly state that it repeals an existing voter-approved right and inaccurately representing the scope of abortion access and the nature of gender transition procedures.
defendant_argument: HJR 73 adheres to the single subject rule because all its provisions are germane to reproductive health care. The revised summary statement and fair ballot language are fair and sufficient to inform voters.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's decision that HJR 73 did not violate the single subject rule but reversed the circuit court's finding that the summary statement and fair ballot language were fair and sufficient, ordering revisions to accurately reflect the measure's effects and avoid misleading voters.

title: Nicholson v. State
description: Whether Senate Bill No. 22 (SB 22) was enacted in violation of the original purpose, single subject, and clear title provisions of the Missouri Constitution, and whether its amendment to section 526.010 violated equal protection.
plaintiff_argument: Nicholson argued SB 22 violated the original purpose, single subject, and clear title requirements of the Missouri Constitution, and that the amendment to section 526.010 violated equal protection.
defendant_argument: The State argued SB 22 satisfied all procedural requirements of the Missouri Constitution and did not violate its equal protection provision.
decision_outcome: The Court reversed the circuit court's judgment, finding that SB 22 violated the Missouri Constitution's original purpose requirement and was unconstitutionally enacted, thus invalidating the bill in its entirety.

title: E.N. v. Kehoe
description: Whether the Missouri SAFE Act and Medicaid ban, which prohibit gender transition surgeries, cross-sex hormones, or puberty-blocking drugs for minors and preclude Medicaid payments for such care, violate the Missouri Constitution's equal protection, due process, and gains of industry clauses.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the SAFE Act and Medicaid ban violate equal protection, due process, and the gains of industry clause of the Missouri Constitution, claiming they classify based on protected classes and infringe on fundamental rights of parents and children.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the SAFE Act and Medicaid ban are constitutionally valid under rational-basis review, as they classify based on age and medical use, serve a legitimate state interest in safeguarding minors, and do not infringe on fundamental rights.
decision_outcome: The circuit court's judgment, upholding the constitutional validity of the SAFE Act and Medicaid ban, is affirmed.

title: State ex rel. Fitz-James v. Bailey
description: Whether the Attorney General has the authority to refuse approval of fiscal note summaries for initiative petitions based on the substance of the fiscal impact assessment, or if his review is limited to "legal content and form".
plaintiff_argument: Dr. Fitz-James argued that the Attorney General's duty to approve fiscal note summaries is ministerial, limited to "legal content and form," and that his refusal to approve based on substantive fiscal impact assessment was an overreach of authority.
defendant_argument: Attorney General Bailey argued that the fiscal notes and summaries were deficient in "legal content and form" due to inadequate responses and underestimated costs, and that his duties were not purely ministerial.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, making permanent the writ of mandamus compelling the Attorney General to approve the fiscal note summaries and notify the Auditor.

title: Robust Missouri Dispensary 3 v. St. Louis County
description: Whether a county may impose a 3 percent sales tax on the sale of non-medical marijuana sold within an incorporated area of the county.
plaintiff_argument: Robust argued that the plain language of the Missouri Constitution specifies that only a village, town, or city in an incorporated area may impose a 3 percent sales tax on non-medical marijuana, not the county.
defendant_argument: The Counties argued that the definition of "local government" in the Missouri Constitution means both a county and a city are "local governments" in an incorporated area, allowing a county to impose the 3 percent sales tax anywhere within its boundaries.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Missouri vacated the circuit court's judgment, ruling that counties cannot impose an additional 3 percent sales tax on non-medical marijuana sold within incorporated cities, towns, or villages.

title: McCarty v. Missouri Secretary of State
description: Whether the summary statement and fiscal note summary for Proposition A were so misleading that they constituted an election irregularity sufficient to cast doubt on the fairness and validity of the election results, and whether Proposition A violated single subject and clear title requirements.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the ballot's summary statement and fiscal note summary for Proposition A were materially inaccurate and seriously misleading, constituting an election irregularity that invalidated the election results. They also claimed Proposition A violated 'single subject' and 'clear title' requirements.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the ballot's summary statement and fiscal note summary were sufficient and fair, and there was no election irregularity. They also contended the court lacked original jurisdiction over the 'single subject' and 'clear title' claims.
decision_outcome: The court found no election irregularity regarding the ballot title for Proposition A, affirmed the validity of the election results, and dismissed the claims regarding 'single subject' and 'clear title' violations for lack of jurisdiction.

title: Coleman v. Ashcroft
description: Whether an initiative petition proposing a constitutional amendment must identify all statutes that might later be declared invalid and whether it violates the single-subject rule.
plaintiff_argument: The petition for Amendment 3 failed to include every constitutional provision and statute that may be altered, invalidated, or otherwise limited or affected, and it violates the single-subject requirement.
defendant_argument: The petition's form was properly approved, the constitution does not require listing all potentially affected statutes, and Amendment 3 adheres to the single-subject rule by focusing on reproductive freedom.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's judgment and ordered Amendment 3 to be placed on the November 2024 general election ballot.

title: State ex rel. Parson v. Walker
description: Whether the current Governor has the authority to rescind a former governor's executive order staying an execution and appointing a board of inquiry, and whether the condemned individual has a due process right to that board of inquiry process.
plaintiff_argument: Marcellus Williams argued that Governor Parson lacked the authority to rescind Executive Order 17-20 and dissolve the board of inquiry before it provided a report and recommendations, and that this action violated his due process rights to a complete review of his claim of innocence.
defendant_argument: Governor Michael L. Parson argued that he had the exclusive constitutional authority to grant or deny clemency, including rescinding a reprieve, and that Williams had no statutory or due process right to the board of inquiry process.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Governor has absolute discretion over clemency and can rescind a reprieve, and that Williams has no cognizable liberty or life interest triggering due process protections during the clemency process, making the preliminary writ of prohibition permanent.

title: Lucas v. Ashcroft
description: Whether the auditor's fiscal note summary for Amendment No. 4 fairly and accurately summarized the auditor's fiscal note as required by section 116.175.3, thereby impacting the validity of the election results.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Quinton Lucas, argued that the fiscal note summary printed on the ballot for Amendment No. 4 materially misstated the fiscal note, rendering it insufficient and unfair, and constituting an irregularity that cast doubt on the fairness and validity of the election results.
defendant_argument: The defendants (Secretary of State and State Auditor) argued that defects in a ballot title cannot form the basis for an election contest, that a pre-election challenge was the exclusive remedy, that the amendment was already effective, and that "irregularities" are limited to election day conduct.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the fiscal note summary for Amendment No. 4 was inaccurate and misleading, setting aside the results of the 2022 general election for Amendment No. 4 and ordering a new election to be conducted on November 5, 2024.

title: Planned Parenthood of the St. Louis Region v. Knodell
description: Whether House Bill No. 3014 (HB 3014), which eliminated Medicaid funding for abortion providers and their affiliates, is unconstitutional, with Planned Parenthood arguing it violates single subject and equal protection clauses, and the State arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: Planned Parenthood argued HB 3014 violated the Missouri Constitution's single subject requirement by combining appropriation with substantive law changes and the equal protection clause by denying funding to Planned Parenthood while other providers received it for similar services.
defendant_argument: The State argued HB 3014 did not violate the single subject or equal protection provisions and that Planned Parenthood lacked standing, waived its claims, and failed to exhaust administrative remedies.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the circuit court's judgment that HB 3014 was unconstitutional, specifically on the equal protection claim, thereby preventing the State from denying Medicaid reimbursement to Planned Parenthood.

title: Faatz v. Ashcroft
description: Whether the Missouri Senate redistricting plan violates constitutional requirements for redistricting, specifically regarding community preservation and equal population.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the Senate Map violates the community preservation requirement by splitting Buchanan County and the City of Hazelwood, and also violates equal population requirements because districts containing these split communities deviate from the ideal population by more than one percent without proper justification. They also contend that compactness should not take priority over community preservation and that mathematical calculations for compactness are inappropriate.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the Senate Map is constitutional, that the circuit court did not err, and that the appellants failed to prove the map unconstitutional. The map prioritizes compactness over community preservation as allowed by the constitution, and any deviations are due to recognized factors like population equality and compactness.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Missouri affirmed the circuit court's judgment, finding that the Missouri Senate redistricting plan is constitutional.

title: The Reverend Traci Blackmon v. Missouri
description: Whether Missouri's statutory abortion restrictions, including the total abortion ban and the declaration that life begins at conception, violate the Establishment Clauses of the Missouri Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argue that these provisions establish particular religious beliefs about the beginning of life, thereby interfering with religious freedom and coercing adherence to specific religious requirements, which violates the Missouri Constitution's Establishment Clauses.
defendant_argument: The state respondents contend that the provisions do not violate the Missouri Constitution, citing historical abortion restrictions, the non-religious nature of the "life begins at conception" determination, and that legislative comments on religious motivations are irrelevant.
decision_outcome: The court granted the State Respondents' motion for judgment on the pleadings, ruling that the challenged abortion provisions do not violate the Missouri Constitution's Establishment Clauses.

title: City of St. Louis v. State
description: Whether Senate Bill No. 26 (SB 26) violates the Missouri Constitution by creating an unfunded mandate, deviating from its original purpose, imposing additional duties on charter cities, improperly granting public funds, and violating equal protection.
plaintiff_argument: SB 26 violates the Missouri Constitution on multiple grounds, including creating an unfunded mandate by requiring new activities without funding, deviating from its original purpose, imposing additional duties on charter city officials, improperly granting public funds to private persons (police officers), and violating equal protection by treating law enforcement officers differently.
defendant_argument: SB 26 is constitutional, arguing it does not create an unfunded mandate, retained its original purpose, does not impose new duties, serves a public purpose in its use of funds, and has a rational basis for treating law enforcement officers differently.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's judgment regarding the unfunded mandate claim (Point II) and remanded the case for further proceedings on that point, while affirming the circuit court's judgment on all other constitutional challenges to SB 26.

title: Fitz-James v. Ashcroft
description: Whether the summary statements prepared by the Missouri Secretary of State for six initiative petitions regarding reproductive freedom were insufficient and unfair, and whether the circuit court erred in redrafting them.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the Secretary's original summary statements for the initiative petitions were insufficient and unfair because they used partisan language and focused too narrowly on abortion, failing to accurately describe the initiatives' full scope.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his original summary statements were fair and sufficient, accurately summarized the initiatives, and that the circuit court erred in finding them insufficient/unfair and in rewriting them entirely.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part the circuit court's judgment, finding that the circuit court had the authority to redraft the summary statements but erred in some specific exclusions, and certified alternative summary statements for the initiative petitions.

title: Byrd v. State
description: Whether Truly Agreed and Finally Passed House Bill 1606 (TAFP HB 1606) violates the single subject requirement of the Missouri Constitution by including provisions on homelessness not germane to political subdivisions.
plaintiff_argument: The Appellants argued that TAFP HB 1606 violated the single subject requirement of the Missouri Constitution because section 67.2300 introduced the impermissible additional subject of homelessness, which was not germane to the bill's stated subject of political subdivisions.
defendant_argument: The Respondents argued that TAFP HB 1606 did not violate the single subject requirement and that all provisions, including section 67.2300, fairly related to the bill's subject of political subdivisions.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's judgment, holding that TAFP HB 1606 violates the single subject requirement of the Missouri Constitution and is invalid in its entirety.

title: Conservation Commission v. Bailey
description: Whether the Missouri Constitution permits the General Assembly to limit the Conservation Commission's authority to expend and use conservation funds for the constitutionally enumerated purposes, with the plaintiff arguing the General Assembly lacks such authority and the defendant arguing the General Assembly's appropriation power allows for such restrictions.
plaintiff_argument: The Conservation Commission argues that Article IV, sections 40-44 of the Missouri Constitution grant it plenary authority to expend and use conservation funds for enumerated purposes without legislative discretion, making the General Assembly's restrictions unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General and Commissioner of the Office of Administration argue that the General Assembly's power of appropriation includes determining the specific amount and purpose of funds, and therefore, its restrictions on the Conservation Commission's use of funds in HB 2019 were valid.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, ruling that the General Assembly lacks the authority to restrict the Conservation Commission from using its funds for constitutionally enumerated purposes, thereby upholding the Conservation Commission's plenary authority.

title: State v. Hamby
description: Whether the circuit court's jury instructions violated the defendant's constitutional right to a unanimous verdict by failing to differentiate between multiple alleged acts of abuse, with the plaintiff arguing no violation occurred and the defendant arguing his right was infringed.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Missouri argued that the jury instructions did not violate the constitutional right to a unanimous verdict because the nature of the evidence abated any risk that the jury did not substantially agree on the same act or acts.
defendant_argument: John A. Hamby argued that the jury instructions violated his constitutional right to a unanimous verdict because they failed to specify distinct acts of abuse, making it unclear which incident the jury found him guilty of.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Missouri affirmed John Hamby's judgment of conviction, finding that the jury instructions preserved his right to a unanimous verdict.

title: State ex rel. Grooms v. Privette
description: Whether a circuit court has the authority to hold an elected circuit clerk in contempt for alleged deficiencies in complying with a court order to prepare a spreadsheet of court costs related to state reimbursements for incarceration, where the plaintiff (Betty Grooms) argues the judge lacks such authority for duties unrelated to the judicial function, and the defendant (Judge Steven A. Privette) argues he has the authority to enforce compliance with statutory duties through contempt.
plaintiff_argument: Betty Grooms argued that Judge Privette lacked the authority to hold her in contempt for alleged deficiencies in complying with a court order regarding statutory administrative duties, as these duties are unrelated to the court's judicial function.
defendant_argument: Judge Steven A. Privette argued that he had the authority to issue the order and enforce compliance through contempt proceedings, as the circuit clerk's duties included preparing bills of costs for state reimbursement of incarceration expenses.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Missouri made the preliminary writ of prohibition permanent, ruling that Judge Privette exceeded his authority by ordering Grooms to show cause why she should not be held in contempt, and ordered the circuit court to dismiss the prosecutor's motion for contempt.

title: Wilson v. City of St. Louis
description: Whether sections 82.485 and 82.487 of the parking statutes are constitutionally invalid because they create powers and duties for municipal offices of the City of St. Louis, a charter city, in violation of article VI, section 22 of the Missouri Constitution, and if so, whether the invalid provisions are severable.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the parking statutes are constitutionally invalid because they create powers and duties for municipal offices in a charter city, violating Article VI, Section 22 of the Missouri Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the parking statutes are constitutionally valid, contending they permissibly fix powers and duties of county offices, not municipal, and that if any provisions are invalid, they are severable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that the parking statutes' provisions creating duties for municipal offices are constitutionally invalid and void, but reversed the circuit court's finding that these provisions were not severable, holding that the invalid parts are severable and the remaining statutes are valid and in effect.

title: Zang v. City of St. Charles
description: Whether the City of St. Charles's charter notice requirement for lawsuits, mandating notice within ninety days of injury, irreconcilably conflicts with state statutes concerning sovereign immunity waivers and statutes of limitations.
plaintiff_argument: Zang argues the City's charter notice requirement is unconstitutional and must be invalidated because it conflicts with state statutes 537.600.1, 82.210, and 516.120.
defendant_argument: The City argues Zang's premises liability claim is barred due to his failure to provide proper notice as required by its Charter, asserting the Charter's notice provision is not inconsistent or in conflict with state law.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, finding no irreconcilable conflict between the City's Charter section 12.3 and the state statutes cited by Zang, thereby upholding the dismissal of Zang's claim.

title: AFSCME v. State
description: Whether Senate Bill No. 1007 (SB 1007) mandates at-will employment for non-merit state employees, thereby restricting their collective bargaining rights and impairing existing collective bargaining agreements, and whether the Personnel Advisory Board's (PAB) implementing rules are authorized and constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The Unions argued that SB 1007 merely creates a default rule for at-will employment, not a mandate, allowing for bargaining over more protective terms, and that SB 1007 violated constitutional rights to collective bargaining and contract, and PAB's rules were unauthorized/unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: The State argued that SB 1007 mandates at-will employment for all non-merit state employees, does not violate constitutional rights to collective bargaining or contract, and that the PAB's amendments are authorized.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's judgment, finding that SB 1007 mandates at-will employment for non-merit state employees, does not infringe on collective bargaining rights or impair contracts, but that many of the PAB's rules are unauthorized expansions of SB 1007.

title: State v. Collins
description: Whether the second-degree harassment statute (section 565.091) is unconstitutionally overbroad in violation of the First and Fourteenth Amendments, and whether sentencing for both tampering with a judicial officer and second-degree harassment violates the right to be free from double jeopardy.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that section 565.091 is not overbroad, there was sufficient evidence to support Collins' harassment conviction, and sentencing for both offenses did not violate double jeopardy.
defendant_argument: Collins argued that section 565.091 is unconstitutionally overbroad, there was insufficient evidence for his harassment conviction, and sentencing for both offenses violated double jeopardy because second-degree harassment is a lesser-included offense of tampering with a judicial officer.
decision_outcome: The circuit court's judgment was affirmed, holding that section 565.091 is not overbroad, there was sufficient evidence for the harassment conviction, and sentencing for both tampering with a judicial officer and second-degree harassment did not violate double jeopardy.

title: All Star Awards & Ad Specialties, Inc. v. HALO Branded Solutions
description: Whether the statutory cap on punitive damages violates the right to a jury trial and whether the reduced punitive damages award violates due process.
plaintiff_argument: All Star argued that the statutory punitive damages cap in section 510.265 violated its right to a jury trial because its common law claims (civil conspiracy to breach duty of loyalty and tortious interference) were analogous to claims existing before 1820 that would have supported unlimited punitive damages.
defendant_argument: HALO argued that the reduced punitive damages award, even after the statutory cap was applied, was still grossly excessive and violated due process.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, upholding the application of the punitive damages cap and finding the reduced award constitutional.

title: Choice v. Ashcroft
description: Whether sections 116.180 and 116.334.2 of Missouri law, which prohibit collecting referendum petition signatures before the official ballot title is certified, unconstitutionally interfere with the right of referendum.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that sections 116.180 and 116.334.2 unconstitutionally interfere with and impede the right of referendum by dramatically reducing the time available for signature collection.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the challenged statutes are constitutionally valid, leave sufficient time for signature gathering, and that the plaintiff failed to demonstrate they are facially invalid.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, declaring sections 116.180 and 116.334.2 unconstitutional because they interfere with and impede the constitutional right of referendum.

title: Velazquez v. University Physician Associates
description: Whether Section 538.210's non-economic damage caps for medical malpractice cases violate Article I, Section 22(a) of the Missouri Constitution, which guarantees the right to trial by jury, with the plaintiff arguing the caps are unconstitutional and the defendant arguing they are constitutional for statutorily created causes of action.
plaintiff_argument: Ordinola argued that the non-economic damage caps contained in § 538.210 violate her constitutional right to trial by jury, and that the higher catastrophic injury cap with the 2019 inflation adjustment should apply.
defendant_argument: The Physicians argued that the non-economic damage caps are constitutional because medical negligence is now a statutorily created cause of action, allowing the legislature to define remedies, and that the standard cap from 2015 should apply.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Missouri affirmed the circuit court's judgment, holding that Section 538.210's non-economic damage caps do not violate the Missouri Constitution and that the catastrophic injury cap with the 2019 inflation adjustment was correctly applied.

title: Doyle v. Tidball
description: Whether article IV, section 36(c) of the Missouri Constitution, which expands MO HealthNet eligibility, violates article III, section 51 by effectively appropriating money or removing the General Assembly's discretion to appropriate funds.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that article IV, section 36(c) is constitutionally valid because it does not expressly appropriate money nor divest the General Assembly of its discretion, and the FY 2022 appropriation bills fund MO HealthNet, guaranteeing their right to coverage.
defendant_argument: The defendant (DSS) argued that it lacked authority to enroll individuals under article IV, section 36(c) because the General Assembly did not specifically fund Medicaid expansion, and the initiative was unconstitutional as it effectively appropriated money without new revenue.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the circuit court's judgment that article IV, section 36(c) was unconstitutional, ruling that the initiative is valid and does not violate article III, section 51, and remanded the case for judgment in favor of the plaintiffs to implement the MO HealthNet expansion.

title: Missorui National Education Association v. Missouri Department of Labor & Industrial Relations
description: Whether House Bill No. 1413, which exempts public safety labor organizations from its provisions, violates the Missouri Constitution's equal protection and collective bargaining rights, and if so, whether the unconstitutional provisions can be severed.
plaintiff_argument: The Labor Unions argued that HB 1413's exemption for public safety labor organizations violates constitutional rights to equal protection and collective bargaining, and that the unconstitutional provisions are not severable, making the entire bill void.
defendant_argument: The State argued that HB 1413 is constitutional, the exemption does not violate equal protection, and if any part is unconstitutional, it should be severed rather than invalidating the entire act.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, declaring HB 1413 void in its entirety and permanently enjoining its administration and enforcement because the exemption for public safety labor organizations violates equal protection and is not severable.

title: City of Crestwood v. Affton Fire Protection District
description: Whether sections 72.418.2 and 321.322.3, governing fire protection services and payment in annexed areas, are unconstitutional special laws, impose an invalid tax on residents, violate due process, or create an unfunded mandate.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that sections 72.418.2 and 321.322.3 are unconstitutional special laws lacking a rational basis, impose an invalid tax on Crestwood residents without voter approval, violate due process rights, and create an unfunded mandate for Crestwood.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the challenged statutes are supported by a rational basis due to the unique annexation risks in St. Louis County, the fee is not a tax on Crestwood residents, it does not violate due process, and it does not create an unfunded mandate as annexation is voluntary.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, finding that the challenged statutes are supported by a rational basis, the fee is not a tax on residents, and it does not create an unfunded mandate.
